label: Chapter 3
name: Time Value of Money: Present Value, Future Value and Annuities

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a reason for the time value (time preference) of money?
o: Money always loses value because of taxes
The presence of risk and uncertainty
A preference to spend for today's needs
The availability of multiple investment options
questions.d: Time value of money: money today is worth more than the same sum in future because of risk and uncertainty, preference to spend now, and multiple options to invest.
questions.w: The three reasons on the slides are risk, present preference and investment options. Taxes are not listed.

questions.q: Discounting means:
o: Converting a future value back to its present value, reversing compounding
Growing a present sum into a future value
Reducing the price of a product
questions.d: Discounting: converting a future value into its present value using a discounting rate. It reverses the effect of compounding.
questions.w: Compounding moves money forward in time; discounting moves it back to today.

questions.q: Ali deposits RO 2,000 at 4% simple interest. How much does he receive after 18 months?
questions.d: Future value with simple interest: Fv = Pv(1 + rt).

questions.q: Rahima deposits RO 5,000 on 1 April 2023 at 6% simple interest for 15 months. When and how much does she receive?
questions.d: Future value with simple interest: Fv = Pv(1 + rt).

questions.q: RO 2,000 is invested for 5 years at 12% compounded monthly. What is the future value?
questions.d: Future value with compound interest: Fv = Pv(1 + r/n)^(nt).

questions.q: For RO 5,000 over 5 years, which is better: 5.5% simple interest or 5% compounded annually?
questions.d: Fv (simple) = Pv(1 + rt); Fv (compound) = Pv(1 + r)^t.
questions.w: Simple: 5,000 × (1 + 0.055 × 5) = RO 6,375.000. Compound: 5,000 × 1.05^5 = RO 6,381.408. Compound is slightly better.

questions.q: RO 10,000 for one year: which gives the higher future value, 10% compounded quarterly or 10.10% compounded annually?
questions.d: Fv = Pv(1 + r/n)^(nt).

questions.q: Ahmed needs RO 50,000 for a car in 5 years. How much must he deposit today at 5% simple interest?
questions.d: Present value with simple interest: Pv = Fv ÷ (1 + rt).

questions.q: How much must be invested today at 15% compounded annually to have RO 2,000 in 3 years?
questions.d: Present value with compound interest: Pv = Fv ÷ (1 + r/n)^(nt).

questions.q: Fatma needs RO 5,000 in 3 years. How much should she invest today at 7% compounded annually?
questions.d: Pv = Fv ÷ (1 + r)^t.

questions.q: Ryle must pay RO 4,000 in 2 years and RO 2,000 in 4 years. At 10% compounded annually, how much must he invest today to cover both?
questions.d: Present value of several future sums = sum of each sum's present value.
questions.w: 4,000 ÷ 1.1^2 = RO 3,305.785; 2,000 ÷ 1.1^4 = RO 1,366.027. Total = RO 4,671.812. Each payment is discounted for its own number of years.

questions.q: If the discounting rate increases, the present value of a fixed future amount:
questions.d: Factors affecting PV: a higher discounting rate gives a lower present value, and vice versa.
questions.w: You divide by (1 + r)^t. A bigger r makes the divisor bigger, so the result is smaller.

questions.q: Holding the rate constant, a longer time period gives:
o: A higher future value and a lower present value
A lower future value and a higher present value
A higher future value and a higher present value
questions.d: Factors: larger time period → higher future value; larger time period → lower present value.
questions.w: More years of compounding increase FV; more years of discounting reduce PV.

questions.q: An annuity whose payments are made at the BEGINNING of each period is:
questions.d: Annuity due: payments at the beginning of each period. Ordinary annuity: payments at the end of each period.
questions.w: Timing of payment is what separates an annuity due from an ordinary annuity.

questions.q: A pension paid every month until the person dies is a:
questions.d: Life annuity: payments for the lifetime of an individual, stopping at death (e.g. pensions).
questions.w: A certain annuity has a fixed period, a perpetual annuity never ends, and a contingent annuity depends on an event such as a marriage.

questions.q: Payments that continue only until a daughter's marriage form a:
questions.d: Contingent annuity: payments depend on the occurrence of an event and stop afterwards.
questions.w: The end date is not fixed; it depends on an event happening, which makes it contingent.

questions.q: An annuity with payments of UNEQUAL amounts is:
questions.d: Based on amount: uniform annuity (equal payments) or variable annuity (unequal payments).
questions.w: Ordinary and due describe timing, not amount.

questions.q: Alice deposits RO 5,000 at the end of each year for 10 years at 5%. What is the present value of this annuity?
questions.d: Present value of an ordinary annuity = I × [1 − (1 + r/n)^(−nt)] ÷ (r/n).

questions.q: Muzna can save RO 1,200 at the end of each year, or RO 100 at the end of each month, for 5 years at 5% (compounded to match). Which gives more?
questions.d: Future value of an ordinary annuity = I × [(1 + r/n)^(nt) − 1] ÷ (r/n).

questions.q: Ameer needs RO 10,000 in 4 years. How much must he invest at the end of each year at 7%?
questions.d: Annuity amount I = Future value ÷ {[(1 + r/n)^(nt) − 1] ÷ (r/n)}.
questions.w: Factor = [(1.07)^4 − 1] ÷ 0.07 = 4.439943. I = 10,000 ÷ 4.439943 = RO 2,252.281. Less than 2,500 because the deposits earn interest.

questions.q: In =FV(rate, nper, pmt, [pv], [type]) for monthly compounding over t years, nper is:
questions.d: Excel FV/PV: rate = r ÷ n (rate per period); nper = t × n (total number of periods).
questions.w: With monthly compounding n = 12, so the number of periods is years × 12.

questions.q: In Excel's PV and FV functions, type = 1 means:
o: Payments are due at the beginning of each period
Payments are due at the end of each period
Interest is compounded once a year
The result is shown as a percentage
questions.d: type: 0 for end-of-period payments (ordinary annuity), 1 for beginning-of-period payments (annuity due).
questions.w: 0 is the default (end of period). 1 switches to the beginning.

questions.q: In practice, present and future values are mainly calculated using simple interest.
questions.d: Present and future value can be found with simple or compound interest, but in practice compound interest is mainly used.
questions.w: The notes say the concept is used mainly with compound interest.

questions.q: A longer time period gives a lower present value.
questions.d: Factors affecting PV: the larger the time period, the lower the present value.
questions.w: Discounting over more years divides by a larger factor (1 + r)^t.

questions.q: An ordinary annuity has payments at the end of each period.
questions.d: Ordinary annuity: payments made at the end of each period.
questions.w: That is the definition; payments at the start would be an annuity due.

questions.q: Azim has RO 8,000 to deposit for 5 years. Option 1: 6% simple interest. Option 2: 6% compounded half-yearly. How much does each option give, and which is better?
questions.d: Fv (simple) = Pv(1 + rt). Fv (compound) = Pv(1 + r/n)^(nt).
questions.w: Option 2 is better because interest earned every half year is added to the balance and then earns interest itself.

questions.q: Ahmed must pay RO 5,000, RO 10,000 and RO 15,000 at the end of years 1, 2 and 3. If the market rate is 6% compounded annually, what lump sum settles all three today?
questions.d: Present value: Pv = Fv ÷ (1 + r)^t.
questions.w: Each payment is discounted for its own number of years, then the present values are added.

questions.q: Khalid needs RO 2,500 for a trip in 3 years. He will save a fixed amount at the end of each month in a scheme paying 5% p.a. (compounded monthly). How much must he save each month?
questions.d: Annuity amount: I = Future value ÷ {[(1 + r/n)^(nt) − 1] ÷ (r/n)}.
questions.w: The target is a future amount, so use the future value of annuity formula and solve for the instalment.

questions.q: You plan to save RO 600 at the end of each year for 4 years at 5%. Alternatively you save RO 50 at the end of each month for 4 years at 5% compounded monthly. Find both amounts and say which is better.
questions.d: Future value of annuity = I × [(1 + r/n)^(nt) − 1] ÷ (r/n).
questions.w: Both options save RO 2,400 in total, but monthly deposits start earning interest earlier.

questions.q: Find the present value of an annuity of RO 1,200 paid at the end of each year for 6 years at 10% p.a. compound interest.
questions.d: Present value of ordinary annuity = I × [1 − (1 + r/n)^(−nt)] ÷ (r/n).
questions.w: Each future payment is worth less today; the formula adds up all six discounted payments in one step.

questions.q: Explain the types of annuities based on amount, time of payment and duration, with an example of each.
questions.a:
Based on amount:
- Uniform annuity: equal payments (e.g. a fixed monthly saving).
- Variable annuity: unequal payments.
Based on time of payment:
- Annuity due: payments at the beginning of each period.
- Ordinary annuity: payments at the end of each period.
Based on duration:
- Certain annuity: fixed period (e.g. until a child turns 18).
- Life annuity: for a person's lifetime (e.g. pensions).
- Perpetual annuity: continues indefinitely (e.g. payments to royals).
- Contingent annuity: depends on an event (e.g. until a daughter's marriage).
questions.d: Annuity: a financial product with a series of payments made at regular intervals over a period of time.
questions.w: The three bases answer three questions: how much is paid, when in the period it is paid, and for how long.
